Since 2015, employers must report to OSHA every work-related **amputation**, **in-patient
hospitalization**, or **loss of an eye** within 24 hours. In this notebook you will explore
those Severe Injury Reports (SIRs). Read the module [README](../README.md) and
[data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.
- Parts marked *ENVH 460/560* are required for graduate students and optional for ENVH 312.

# Part 0. Load the data

The file in `data/tidy/` contains **every** report (not a sample) and is committed to the
repository. To refresh it, run `scripts/fetch_data.R` and then `scripts/build_dataset.R`.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

local_path <- "../data/tidy/severe_injury_reports.csv.gz"
github_url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                     "main/modules/us-osha-severe-injury/data/tidy/severe_injury_reports.csv.gz")

sir <- read_csv(if (file.exists(local_path)) local_path else github_url,
                col_types = cols(event_date = col_date(), year = col_integer(), month = col_integer(),
                                 latitude = col_double(), longitude = col_double(),
                                 hospitalized = col_integer(), amputation = col_integer(),
                                 loss_of_eye = col_integer(), .default = col_character()))

cat(format(nrow(sir), big.mark = ","), "reports from", format(min(sir$event_date)), "to",
    format(max(sir$event_date)), "\n")
```

# Part 1. Get oriented

```{r orient}
glimpse(sir)

sir |>
  summarise(reports = n(),
            workers_hospitalized = sum(hospitalized, na.rm = TRUE),
            workers_with_amputation = sum(amputation, na.rm = TRUE),
            workers_with_eye_loss = sum(loss_of_eye, na.rm = TRUE),
            share_inspected = mean(!is.na(inspection)))
```

**Questions**

1. What does one row represent? Can one report involve more than one injured worker?
2. These data cover only workplaces under **federal OSHA** jurisdiction. Which states run
   their own OSHA-approved State Plans? How does that limit what you can conclude about the US?
3. About what share of reports led to an OSHA inspection? What do you think happens to the rest?
   (Hint: look up OSHA's "rapid response investigation".)

**Your answer:**



# Part 2. When do severe injuries happen?

```{r when}
ggplot(count(sir, year), aes(year, n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Severe injury reports per year", x = NULL, y = "Reports")

sir |>
  filter(year < max(year)) |>
  count(month) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(month.abb[month], levels = month.abb), n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Severe injury reports by month (complete years only)", x = NULL, y = "Reports")
```

**Questions**

1. Describe the trend across years. What happened in 2020? Is the most recent year complete?
2. Which months have the most reports? Suggest a reason (see Part 6).

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. What happened?

Each report is coded with the **Occupational Injury and Illness Classification System (OIICS)**,
the same system BLS uses: the *event* (how the injury happened), the *nature* (what the injury
was), the *part of body*, and the *source* (what directly caused it).

```{r what, fig.height = 6}
count(sir, event_division, sort = TRUE)

sir |>
  count(event, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(str_trunc(event, 60), n))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Most common events", x = "Reports", y = NULL)

count(sir, nature, sort = TRUE) |> head(10)
count(sir, body_part, sort = TRUE) |> head(10)
count(sir, source, sort = TRUE) |> head(10)
```

**Questions**

1. Which event divisions account for most severe injuries?
2. What are the most common injuries and body parts? What does that suggest about the
   types of hazards behind severe injuries?
3. Read the `source` list. Which sources are equipment that engineering controls (such as machine
   guarding) could address?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Where and in which industries?

```{r where, fig.height = 6}
count(sir, state, sort = TRUE) |> head(15)

sir |>
  count(naics_2, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(12)
```

NAICS sectors: 23 = construction, 31 to 33 = manufacturing, 48 to 49 = transportation and
warehousing, 44 to 45 = retail trade, 56 = administrative and waste services, 62 = health care.

```{r map}
sir |>
  filter(!is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude)) |>
  ggplot(aes(longitude, latitude)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.3) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-125, -66), ylim = c(24, 50)) +
  labs(title = "Locations of severe injury reports (contiguous US)", x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which states and industries report the most severe injuries? Why is a count of reports not
   the same as a measure of risk?
2. Look at the map. Which parts of the country are nearly empty, and why?

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. Data quality

Real data are messy. The same employer can appear under many spellings:

```{r quality}
sir |>
  filter(str_detect(employer, regex("postal", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  count(employer, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)

# How precise are the coordinates? Are any clearly wrong?
head(sort(unique(sir$latitude)), 10)
sir |> filter(latitude < 15 | longitude > 0) |> select(employer, city, state, latitude, longitude)
```

**Questions**

1. How many spellings of the US Postal Service can you find? Write code that groups them into
   one employer, and count its total reports. Which other large employers might have the same problem?
2. The coordinates have only two decimal places. About how far apart are two points that
   differ by 0.01 degree of latitude? What does that mean for mapping? Some coordinates are
   clearly wrong (for example a latitude of 0). How would you find and handle them?
3. Employers must report these injuries, but studies suggest many are never reported. Who
   might be less likely to report, and why?

**Your answer:**



# Part 6 (ENVH 460/560). Heat-related injuries

```{r heat}
heat <- sir |>
  filter(str_detect(event, regex("environmental heat", ignore_case = TRUE)))

cat(nrow(heat), "reports of exposure to environmental heat\n")

heat |>
  count(year, month) |>
  ggplot(aes(month, n, group = year, colour = factor(year))) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  labs(title = "Heat-related severe injury reports by month", x = NULL, y = "Reports", colour = "Year")

count(heat, naics_2, sort = TRUE) |> head(8)
count(heat, state, sort = TRUE) |> head(8)

heat |> select(event_date, state, narrative) |> slice_sample(n = 5)
```

**Questions**

1. When and where do heat-related severe injuries happen? Which industries are most affected?
2. Read some narratives. What tasks and conditions are involved? What controls (water, rest,
   shade, acclimatization) could have prevented them?
3. Heat illnesses are often not recognized as work-related. Do you think these reports capture
   most heat-related hospitalizations of workers? Why or why not?

**Your answer:**



# Part 7 (ENVH 460/560). Amputations

```{r amputations}
amputations <- sir |> filter(amputation > 0)

count(amputations, naics_2, sort = TRUE) |> head(8)
count(amputations, source, sort = TRUE) |> head(12)
count(amputations, body_part, sort = TRUE) |> head(6)

sir |>
  group_by(had_amputation = coalesce(amputation, 0L) > 0) |>
  summarise(reports = n(), share_inspected = mean(!is.na(inspection)))
```

**Questions**

1. Which industries and sources account for most amputations? How does that relate to OSHA's
   machine guarding standards (29 CFR 1910.212 and 1910.147, lockout/tagout)?
2. Are reports involving amputations more or less likely to be inspected than other reports?
   Why might OSHA prioritize them?
3. OSHA runs a National Emphasis Program on amputations in manufacturing. How could you use
   these data to evaluate whether it works? What would you need besides these data?

**Your answer:**

These data contain **numbers of reports** but no information on how many people work in each
industry or state.
